title: The Bank Covenant You Signed and Then Stopped Watching
linkedin:
Loan approved. Documents signed. Most owners never open that facility agreement again, until something forces a look.

Buried a few pages in sit the covenants the bank attached as a condition of lending: a minimum interest cover ratio, a ceiling on debt against EBITDA, sometimes a requirement to get consent before taking on further debt anywhere else. At settlement, they get read once, filed, and treated as a hurdle already cleared.

They're not. A covenant applies for the life of the facility and gets tested every reporting period, whether anyone is watching it or not.

Here's the part that catches owners out. A covenant breach and a missed repayment are two different events. A business can be current on every single instalment and still be in technical default because a ratio drifted past its threshold. A slow quarter, a customer paying sixty days instead of thirty, or a second piece of equipment finance taken on with a different lender, can be enough.

A breach doesn't automatically mean the loan gets called in. But it hands the bank rights it didn't have the day before: reprice the facility, request more security, ask for an equity injection, reduce the limit. Even the milder outcomes cost real money and management time nobody budgeted for.

The fix isn't complicated. Pull the current interest cover and leverage position against the covenant thresholds at least quarterly, and again after any new debt is added anywhere in the business. It's usually a one-hour exercise against management accounts that already exist.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

If your business is carrying a bank loan, an overdraft or any other facility, it is worth knowing what is actually written into the fine print beyond the interest rate and repayment schedule. Most facilities come with covenants attached, conditions like a minimum interest cover ratio or a ceiling on debt measured against earnings, that the bank set at approval and keeps testing for the life of the loan.

We see business owners across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria treat these as a box ticked at settlement rather than an ongoing condition. That gap matters, because a business can make every repayment on time and still be in technical breach if one of those ratios has drifted since the loan was signed. A quieter trading quarter, a slower-paying customer or extra finance taken on with a different lender can be enough, and a breach hands the bank rights it did not have the day before, from a higher margin through to requesting extra security.

The good news is this is easy to stay ahead of once you know to look. Checking your current position against your facility conditions once a quarter, and again whenever new debt is added anywhere in the business, is usually a short exercise against numbers you already have.

If it has been a while since anyone checked, read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for what to look at first.
